title: What CityAir is
text: CityAir is an independent, open air-quality readiness and innovation-exchange platform for city teams. It has four core functions: (1) a twelve-domain readiness assessment scored from self-reported answers, (2) a city explorer with illustrative profiles and live readings, (3) an innovation implementation library with explainable matching, and (4) an AI assistant grounded in this knowledge base. CityAir is a prototype. It is not an official product of AQMx, CCAC, WRI, NASA, XPRIZE or the World Health Organization, it does not rank or certify cities, and demonstration city data is illustrative.

title: Limits, disclaimers and responsible use
text: CityAir must not be used as a certification, audit, compliance check or official ranking. Illustrative city scores are synthetic demonstration values and must never be quoted as facts about a real city. AI answers are machine generated from a prototype knowledge base and can be incomplete or wrong. Live air-quality readings come from a third-party open API (Open-Meteo) and are model-based, not quality-assured regulatory measurements. Satellite and remote-sensing products must not be presented as direct methane quantification or as verification of emission reductions. Assessment answers stay in the user's browser unless the user explicitly exports them.

title: How the readiness score is calculated
text: Each of the twelve questions belongs to one domain and carries a weight between 0.8 and 1.2. A scored answer from 0 (absent) to 4 (leading) is normalised: (answer / 4) * 100. The domain score is the weighted mean of its questions: sum(normalised * weight) / sum(weight). The overall readiness score is the weighted mean of the domain scores that were actually answered. Answers marked "unknown" or "not applicable" are excluded from both numerator and denominator, so honest gaps reduce completeness rather than silently lowering the score. Maturity bands: Starting 0-34, Developing 35-54, Established 55-69, Advanced 70-84, Leading 85-100. Scores are planning prompts, not certifications.

title: Evidence confidence model
text: Evidence confidence is a 0-100 figure built from three components: 60% confirmed evidence systems (nine source types: regulatory monitoring stations, low-cost sensors, emissions inventories, satellite data, waste-site data, methane measurements, health data, public reporting systems, verified historical records); 25% the share of scored answers that carry an evidence note or link; 15% questionnaire completeness across the twelve domains. A high score with low confidence is the most common self-assessment failure mode: the practice may exist informally and not survive staff turnover. Fewer than 60% of domains scored triggers an insufficient-evidence warning.

title: The five stages of air-quality management capacity
text: 1 Diagnose — frame the problem and the mandate: agree ownership, pollutants, areas and the decisions the evidence must support. 2 Measure — build a trustworthy evidence base: quality-assured monitoring, documented QA/QC, reference stations, sensors and satellite screening combined honestly. 3 Attribute — identify sources and exposure: emissions inventories, dispersion analysis and health evidence so measures can target dominant sources. 4 Act — prioritise, implement and fund: turn evidence into phased measures with owners, budgets, legal instruments and feedback loops. 5 Sustain — communicate, evaluate and iterate: publish results accessibly, evaluate effectiveness and institutionalise improvement.

title: How the phased action plan is generated
text: The action plan uses the lowest-scoring domains and the city's recorded priorities. Phase 1 (0-6 months) stabilises the evidence base: owners, scope, inventory of existing data, QA/QC and completeness notes, and a workshop to confirm priorities. Phase 2 (6-18 months) closes analytical gaps: connect measurements to source attribution, set measurable indicators per priority sector, prepare a costed funding case, and establish a monthly evidence-decision review. Phase 3 (18-36 months) scales, communicates and institutionalises: publish an annual progress report, evaluate delivered measures, re-run the assessment every 12-24 months, and exchange results with peer cities. Every action needs a named owner, a costed option set, a legal or procurement route, an indicator with a baseline and a review date.

title: WHO air-quality guideline reference levels
text: Reference levels (micrograms per cubic metre except CO in mg/m3, from the WHO global air-quality guidelines): PM2.5 annual: interim targets 35, 25, 15, 10; guideline level 5. PM2.5 24-hour: interim targets 75, 50, 37.5, 25; guideline level 15. PM10 annual: interim targets 70, 50, 30, 20; guideline level 15. PM10 24-hour: interim targets 150, 100, 75, 50; guideline level 45. Ozone peak season: interim targets 100, 70; guideline level 60. Ozone 8-hour: interim targets 160, 120; level 100. NO2 annual: interim targets 40, 30, 20; guideline level 10. NO2 24-hour: interim targets 120, 50; level 25. SO2 24-hour: interim targets 125, 50; guideline level 40. CO 24-hour: interim target 7; guideline level 4. Always confirm current values with the WHO source before regulatory use.

title: Core air-quality concepts used by the platform
text: PM2.5 and PM10 are particulate matter with diameters below 2.5 and 10 micrometres; the smaller fraction penetrates deeper into the lungs and bloodstream and dominates health burden in most cities. NO2 is largely traffic- and combustion-related; ozone is formed photochemically and peaks in warm sunny conditions; SO2 is associated with sulphur-bearing fuels and some industry; CO comes from incomplete combustion. Source attribution combines emissions inventories, dispersion and chemical-transport modelling, receptor modelling, speciation and meteorology. Ambient concentrations depend on emissions plus meteorology and topography, which is why valleys and basins show severe winter episodes and why dust events must be separated from managed sources. Exposure is not the same as concentration: it also depends on where people live, work and travel.

title: Guidance domain: Air Quality Monitoring
text: Build a fit-for-purpose, quality-assured picture of ambient pollution. Guiding questions: Which pollutants and places matter most? | How is quality assurance documented?. Recommended actions: Define monitoring objectives | Design representative sites | Publish QA and completeness metrics. Data the domain needs: Reference observations | Site metadata | Calibration and maintenance logs. Maturity sequence: Map needs -> Pilot measurements -> Operate QA system -> Optimize network -> Share interoperable evidence. Public references: AQMx, WHO air-quality guidance.

title: Guidance domain: Source Attribution
text: Identify source contributions using multiple, converging lines of evidence. Guiding questions: Which sources drive exposure? | How do contributions change by season?. Recommended actions: Develop a study plan | Combine inventory and measurement evidence | Document uncertainty. Data the domain needs: Pollutant speciation | Meteorology | Activity data. Maturity sequence: Form hypotheses -> Gather evidence -> Run analysis -> Validate findings -> Update routinely. Public references: AQMx sectoral guidance.

title: Guidance domain: Emissions Inventory
text: Estimate emissions consistently enough to guide and evaluate policy. Guiding questions: Which sectors dominate? | When was the inventory updated?. Recommended actions: Set scope and base year | Collect activity factors | Quality-check and publish. Data the domain needs: Activity data | Emission factors | Spatial proxies. Maturity sequence: Scope -> Compile -> Quality assure -> Use in scenarios -> Institutionalize updates. Public references: AQMx sectoral guidance.

title: Guidance domain: Air Quality Forecasting
text: Anticipate episodes and communicate uncertainty for timely action. Guiding questions: Who needs forecasts? | How is performance evaluated?. Recommended actions: Define use cases | Pilot models | Verify forecasts and alerts. Data the domain needs: Observations | Meteorology | Emissions inputs. Maturity sequence: Define -> Pilot -> Validate -> Operationalize -> Continuously improve. Public references: AQMx.

title: Guidance domain: Health Impact Assessment
text: Connect pollution exposure with health burdens and policy benefits. Guiding questions: Which populations are most exposed? | Which outcomes can be assessed responsibly?. Recommended actions: Engage health authorities | Select validated methods | Communicate uncertainty. Data the domain needs: Population | Exposure surfaces | Baseline health rates. Maturity sequence: Align partners -> Assemble data -> Estimate impacts -> Evaluate interventions -> Embed health evidence. Public references: WHO guidelines.

title: Guidance domain: Environmental Impact Assessment
text: Assess and manage air impacts of plans and projects before approval. Guiding questions: Are cumulative impacts included? | Are mitigations enforceable?. Recommended actions: Set assessment rules | Review baseline evidence | Monitor commitments. Data the domain needs: Project emissions | Baseline concentrations | Sensitive receptors. Maturity sequence: Set criteria -> Build review capacity -> Track mitigations -> Audit outcomes -> Improve standards. Public references: National EIA guidance.

title: Guidance domain: Decision Support
text: Turn evidence into transparent choices, budgets and measurable action. Guiding questions: Who owns decisions? | How are trade-offs documented?. Recommended actions: Create a shared evidence register | Compare measures | Track decisions and outcomes. Data the domain needs: Costs | Benefits | Distributional impacts. Maturity sequence: Map decisions -> Organize evidence -> Compare options -> Track outcomes -> Institutionalize learning. Public references: GreenHope methodology.

title: Guidance domain: Public Engagement and Communication
text: Enable residents to understand risks, contribute knowledge and act. Guiding questions: Which audiences are underserved? | Are messages tested?. Recommended actions: Co-design communication | Use accessible channels | Evaluate comprehension. Data the domain needs: Audience research | Alert reach | Feedback. Maturity sequence: Listen -> Prototype -> Publish -> Evaluate -> Co-govern. Public references: WHO health communication.

title: Guidance domain: Legal Framework and Policy Design
text: Clarify mandates, standards, accountability and enforceable clean-air measures. Guiding questions: Are responsibilities clear? | Can standards be enforced fairly?. Recommended actions: Map legal powers | Close mandate gaps | Publish accountability measures. Data the domain needs: Legal instruments | Compliance records | Policy evaluations. Maturity sequence: Map framework -> Clarify roles -> Implement policy -> Evaluate compliance -> Update adaptively. Public references: AQMx.

title: Guidance domain: Waste Management
text: Reduce air and climate harms through controlled, inclusive waste systems. Guiding questions: Where does waste flow? | Which sites lack controls?. Recommended actions: Build a site register | Prioritize risks | Improve collection and controls. Data the domain needs: Waste flows | Site operations | Inspection records. Maturity sequence: Map -> Stabilize -> Control -> Optimize -> Recover resources. Public references: AQMx sectoral guidance.

title: Guidance domain: Open Waste Burning
text: Prevent burning through detection, viable services and coordinated response. Guiding questions: Why does burning occur? | How are reports validated?. Recommended actions: Map recurrence | Provide alternatives | Track response and recurrence. Data the domain needs: Community reports | Fire screening | Local PM measurements. Maturity sequence: Identify -> Validate -> Respond -> Prevent -> Sustain zero-burning systems. Public references: NASA FIRMS caveats, AQMx sectoral guidance.

title: Guidance domain: Methane and Landfill Monitoring
text: Screen landfill-gas risks, then quantify and verify with suitable measurements. Guiding questions: Which sites need qualified measurement? | How will mitigation be verified?. Recommended actions: Review site operations | Plan safe measurement | Verify mitigation over time. Data the domain needs: Waste composition | Site geometry | Ground or airborne methane measurements. Maturity sequence: Screen -> Measure -> Diagnose -> Mitigate -> Verify. Public references: XPRIZE Mission Methane reference.

title: Innovation brief: Tiered Landfill Methane Screening
text: Sector: Methane. Status: Illustrative GreenHope demonstration. Region: Adaptable. Problem addressed: Limited visibility of landfill-gas risks and emission hotspots Required capacity: Developing. Required data: Waste-site boundaries; Operational records; Appropriate ground or airborne methane measurements. Benefits: Prioritizes measurement and mitigation resources without overstating remote observations. title: Where is assessment data stored?
text: Assessment answers, evidence notes and priorities are stored only in your browser's localStorage under the key cityair-assessment-v1. Nothing is uploaded unless you export the JSON file or explicitly send a summary to the AI assistant. There are no accounts and no third-party analytics.

title: How the AI assistant is built
text: The assistant retrieves the most relevant passages from the published CityAir knowledge base (BM25 keyword retrieval with an embeddings rerank where an inference provider is available), then asks a language model to answer only from those passages and returns the passages it used as sources. If the language model is unavailable, the assistant returns the retrieved passages verbatim instead of inventing an answer, so the service degrades to a search interface rather than failing or hallucinating. The knowledge base is published as an open dataset on Hugging Face, and the API runs as a Cloudflare Worker.

title: The Telegram air tracker bot
text: The companion Telegram bot reports current PM2.5, PM10 and European AQI for any city using the open Open-Meteo air-quality API, answers knowledge-base questions, and links back to the platform. Commands: /start, /aqi <city>, /city <name>, /ask <question>, /help, /about. Readings are model-based and are not quality-assured regulatory measurements.

title: Comparing cities fairly
text: City profiles use the same twelve domains so comparisons are structurally fair, but context differs: baseline meteorology, topography, industrial history and data availability all shape what is achievable. A lower score in a difficult setting can represent more honest reporting than a higher score with weak evidence, which is exactly why the evidence-confidence figure accompanies every score. Comparisons are for peer learning, not league tables.

title: How to start using CityAir
text: 1 Read the twelve guidance domains to understand what capacity looks like. 2 Open the assessment and complete city context, then score the domains you can evidence. 3 Review the readiness dashboard: score, band, evidence confidence and priority gaps. 4 Generate the phased action plan and attach owners, costs and review dates. 5 Use innovation matching to find implementation options that fit your capacity. 6 Ask the assistant to explain any result, and re-run the assessment every 12-24 months.

title: Cooperation models with CityAir and the AQMx pathway (ISAF Smartex 2026)
text: 1 · City pilot with a documented evidence trail: WITH CITYAIR — The company provides sensors, connectivity or a platform for one district; CityAir provides the 12-domain readiness baseline, the evidence-confidence framework, the public dashboard text and the impact indicators. We publish what worked and what did not. WITH AQMX — undefined WE ASK — One pilot city, 3–6 sensors, 6 months, one agreed indicator set WE GIVE — Independent assessment, transparent publication, no hidden endorsement 2 · Data and interoperability: WITH CITYAIR — Their operational data (traffic counts, waste routes, building energy, gas detection) is mapped into CityAir's twelve domains so the assessment can cite real evidence instead of self-declared answers. WITH AQMX — undefined WE ASK — A documented data schema + a named data owner + an update cycle WE GIVE — A public evidence register entry with provenance and quality notes 3 · Co-authored innovation brief: WITH CITYAIR — The company submits a solution; CityAir co-authors the brief in the library template: problem, required capacity, required data, delivery steps, risks, adaptation notes, monitoring indicators. WITH AQMX — undefined WE ASK — One product, one honest limitation statement, one reference deployment WE GIVE — Publication with full attribution and a link to the company 4 · Sponsorship with a firewall: WITH CITYAIR — A company can fund an assessment cycle, a methane-screening study or a workshop series. Sponsors never set scores, never edit findings and are named as funders only. WITH AQMX — undefined WE ASK — Funding with a written conflict-of-interest clause WE GIVE — Public acknowledgement, no influence over results or rankings 5 · Capacity building and training: WITH CITYAIR — Joint webinars and municipal workshops in Turkish, English and Persian on reading evidence quality, procurement of monitoring and communicating air-quality risk. WITH AQMX — undefined WE ASK — Two experts and a venue or a webinar slot WE GIVE — Trilingual materials, recorded sessions, a certificate of participation for municipal staff 6 · Independent evaluation partnership: WITH CITYAIR — Before-and-after indicator tracking on a deployed system, with baseline, method and uncertainty stated in public. WITH AQMX — undefined WE ASK — Access to the deployment's operational data and permission to publish WE GIVE — Third-party evaluation with a stated method — the strongest sales argument a vendor can hold Important: the AQMx column describes how a company COULD contribute to the AQMx knowledge exchange. title: Fair outreach kit: booth script, follow-up and field checklist
text: Booth visit — 20-second opener (English): Hello — I am with CityAir (aqmx.atikova.com), an independent platform that scores how ready a city actually is to use air-quality technology, and publishes implementation briefs. We are not selling sensors; we are building the evidence layer that makes your deployments defensible. Two questions: (1) do you have a municipal reference deployment in Türkiye we could document together, and (2) would you fund a six-month independent evaluation with published results? Here is a one-page brief and my card. Stant ziyareti — 20 saniyelik giriş (Türkçe): Merhaba — ben CityAir'den (aqmx.atikova.com). Bağımsız bir platformuz: bir şehrin hava kalitesi teknolojisini gerçekten kullanmaya ne kadar hazır olduğunu puanlıyor ve uygulama brifleri yayımlıyoruz. Sensör satmıyoruz; yatırımınızı savunulabilir kılan kanıt katmanını kuruyoruz. İki soru: (1) Türkiye'de birlikte belgeleyebileceğimiz bir belediye referans kurulumunuz var mı, (2) altı aylık bağımsız bir değerlendirmeyi ve sonuçların yayımlanmasını finanse eder misiniz? title: XPRIZE Mission Methane — what the competition is and how CityAir fits
text: XPRIZE Mission Methane targets diffuse, low-concentration methane emissions that conventional mitigation misses — landfills, wastewater systems, agriculture, wetlands and the atmosphere — across four intervention categories: prevention, mitigation, destruction and atmospheric removal. It is modelled on the proven XPRIZE Carbon Removal structure and, at the time of writing, sits in the partner-development phase; prize fund, timeline and final criteria are whatever XPRIZE announces, and must never be presented as fixed. CityAir's fit: the evidence layer, not the technology. Ground-validated hotspot detection (matching satellite and thermal alerts against sensor networks and publishing the false-positive rate), a documented methane and PM2.5 baseline that separates measured from modelled from unknown, an independent evaluation method with confidence scoring, a civil-society partner for community data, and open publication of method and data so a reviewer can reproduce the result. Sequencing: confirm one technical partner and one civil-society partner first (MoveGreen is the candidate), produce one documented pilot result, then approach the official channel. No announcement before the first published output. Source: https://www.xprize.org/competitions/methane

title: Cooperation plan with MoveGreen — five workstreams, 90-day map, asks and risks
text: Principle: MoveGreen is the local evidence authority; CityAir is the technical and publishing layer. Neither side claims the other's work, and every published number carries its method and its limits. Five workstreams: (1) validate Earth-observation and thermal alerts with ground sensors — deliver a validation note including the false-positive rate (weeks 1–6); (2) map waste-burning and landfill environmental-risk hotspots into a public register with provenance for every entry (weeks 1–8); (3) develop the methane and PM2.5 baseline as a baseline statement that separates measured, modelled and unknown (weeks 4–12); (4) connect a waste-management or landfill operator and sign a site-level data agreement (weeks 4–14); (5) responsible public communication and citizen engagement, led by MoveGreen, with trilingual materials and the Telegram bot for field reports (weeks 6–14). CityAir adds: the twelve-domain readiness assessment producing the first fully evidenced Bishkek record, evidence-confidence scoring, innovation briefs with required data and risks, public dashboard templates and print exports, and open publication of the knowledge base and method. MoveGreen brings: the 100+ sensor PM network, the AQ.kg app and its audience, citizen-engagement capacity, media and advocacy reach, and convening power through the Central Asian Air Quality Platform. Ninety-day map: days 1–14 send the concept note, hold the introductory call, agree the pilot district and focal points, confirm data-sharing terms in writing; days 15–45 run the EO-versus-ground validation on historical data, draft the hotspot register, open the waste-operator conversation; days 46–90 publish the validation note and baseline statement, deliver the communication pack, package the case study for the AQMx exchange and COP31. Five asks: one pilot district with a named focal point; historical PM data for that district; one introduction to a waste-management or landfill operator; written agreement on what may be published (MoveGreen holds veto over anything describing their own network); two hours per week of technical time from one staff member. Risks and mitigations: methane is not MoveGreen's current workstream and could overload a small team — CityAir carries the methane method; satellite alerts are already over-claimed in this field — publish the false-positive rate and state that remote sensing screens rather than quantifies; a premature partnership announcement damages both sides — no announcement before the first published output; third-party personal data could leak into a public repository — publish roles and organisational contacts only.
